candidate_sources.title: Alfalfa mosaic virus - Wikipedia
candidate_sources.snippet: Alfalfa mosaic virus (AMV) is a plant virus with a broad host range including soybean, alfalfa, clover, snap bean, and pea. It causes bright yellow mosaic leaves and vein yellowing. Symptoms vary from wilting, white flecks, malformation, dwarfing, ringspots, mottles, mosaics to necrosis depending on virus strain and environmental conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Alfalfa Mosaic Developing in a Few Alfalfa Fields
candidate_sources.snippet: South Dakota State University Extension resource on Alfalfa Mosaic Virus development and management in alfalfa fields, with relevance to soybean as a secondary host.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean mosaic virus (soybean mosaic) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium comprehensive reference on soybean viruses including Alfalfa Mosaic Virus as a pathogen affecting soybean crops, with detailed pathogen characteristics, symptomatology, transmission vectors, and management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose causes irregular brown to reddish-brown lesions on stems, petioles, and pods. Infected areas are covered with tiny black spines (setae) visible with a hand lens. The pathogen Colletotrichum truncatum overwinters in crop residue and infected seeds. Warm, moist conditions favor disease development and premature defoliation may occur.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Anthracnose of soybean is characterized by symptoms on stems, pods, and petioles including red to brown dark irregular lesions. Infected petioles may display a 'shepherd's crook' appearance. The fungal pathogen causes seedborne and residue-borne inoculum. Management includes use of disease-free seed, resistant varieties, and crop rotation.

candidate_sources.title: Anthracnose in Soybean | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Soybean anthracnose causes lesions with small black fruiting bodies (acervuli) on affected plant parts. Primary causal agent is Colletotrichum truncatum. Disease management recommendations include certified disease-free seed, crop rotation away from susceptible crops, and variety selection with resistance or tolerance to anthracnose.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial blight on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Infections begin as small, angular, water-soaked spots that turn yellow and then brown as the tissue dies. Caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. glycinea. Management includes resistant varieties, crop rotation, pathogen-free seed, and avoiding field cultivation when foliage is wet.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Blight of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Light to dark brown necrotic regions, vein-limited with angular appearance on young leaves with chlorosis. Can occur on all above-ground plant parts but most evident on leaves in mid to upper canopy. Development promoted by cool, wet weather (70-80°F).

candidate_sources.title: Chapter 58: Bacterial Diseases of Soybeans - SDSU Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive chapter on bacterial diseases of soybeans including detailed symptomatology, pathogen biology, epidemiology, and management recommendations for bacterial blight and other bacterial pathogens.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial pustule on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial pustule causes small light green spots with raised centers on leaves and pods. The disease is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. glycines and is favored by warm, wet weather. The disease can occur at any time during the growing season.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Pustule | CropWatch - University of Nebraska–Lincoln
candidate_sources.snippet: Bacterial pustule is distinguished by tan pustules on the undersides of leaves and lack of water soaking at initial infection sites. The pathogen is Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. glycines. Management includes use of resistant varieties and crop rotation.

candidate_sources.title: Bacterial Pustule - Soybean Disease - Soybean Research & Information Network (SRIN)
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive resource on bacterial pustule of soybean covering symptom identification, pathogen biology (Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. glycines), and integrated disease management strategies for soybean production.

candidate_sources.title: Bean pod mottle virus on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Bean pod mottle virus causes green to yellow mottling of young leaves, leaf distortion, and stunting. BPMV is transmitted by leaf-feeding beetles, specifically the bean leaf beetle. The virus can cause yield losses as high as 52% and reduce seed quality, with higher losses when co-infected with Soybean mosaic virus.

candidate_sources.title: Bean Pod Mottle Virus | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Bean pod mottle virus (BPMV) is a member of the genus Comovirus in the family Comoviridae. Symptoms include mild to severe chlorotic mottling or mosaic, rugosity (wrinkling) on foliage and pods, stunting, and delayed maturity. Infected seed can be discolored or mottled. Management strategies include resistant varieties and beetle control.

candidate_sources.title: Bean Pod Mottle Virus | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Bean pod mottle virus affects soybean production with visual symptoms including chlorotic mottle, leaf distortion, and pod mottling. Transmission occurs through bean leaf beetle vectors. Economic impact includes reduced yields and seed quality degradation in infected fields.

candidate_sources.title: Brown Spot of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Brown spot is caused by Septoria glycines. Symptoms include light to dark brown necrotic regions on the lower leaves of the plant, often with chlorosis surrounding the lesions. Initial symptoms are small dark brown spots (less than 1/8 inch in size). The brown spots often enlarge and grow together into irregular brown areas. Under warm, wet conditions, the fungus spreads via asexual spores. Management includes crop rotation, residue incorporation, and fungicide applications during R3-R5 growth stages.

candidate_sources.title: Septoria brown spot | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Septoria brown spot is one of the most common foliar diseases of soybeans, caused by Septoria glycines. Initial symptoms are small dark brown spots (less than 1/8 inch) appearing first on lower leaves, progressing upward. Temperatures between 60-85°F and prolonged wet periods favor disease development. Yield losses typically range from 5-8% under severe conditions. Management includes crop rotation to non-host crops (corn, alfalfa, small grains), residue incorporation, and foliar fungicides applied during R3-R5 growth stages.

candidate_sources.title: Septoria Brown Spot in Soybean | University of Delaware Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Septoria brown spot, caused by the fungus Septoria glycines, is characterized by small dark brown spots on soybean leaves that enlarge into irregular brown patches with yellow halos. The pathogen survives on crop residue and spreads via wind and water-splash. Disease development is favored by temperatures of 60-85°F and extended leaf wetness periods. Management strategies include resistant varieties where available, crop rotation to non-legumes, incorporation of infested residue, and timely fungicide applications.

candidate_sources.title: Brown stem rot (BSR) on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Brown stem rot causes browning of the pith in the center of the stem, especially near the lower nodes. The pathogen is Phialophora gregata (also named Cadophora gregata), a soilborne fungus. Two different types cause different symptoms - Type A causes pith browning and leaf symptoms, Type B causes only pith browning. Management includes resistant varieties and crop rotation.

candidate_sources.title: OSU Soybean Diseases - Brown Stem Rot Extended Version
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive guide to Brown Stem Rot in soybean including detailed symptom descriptions, disease cycle, environmental factors favoring disease development, and management recommendations including variety selection and rotation strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Brown Stem Rot - Soybean Disease - Soybean Research & Information Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Dedicated resource page for Brown Stem Rot disease covering symptoms, pathogen biology, environmental conditions favoring infection, and integrated management practices for soybean production.

candidate_sources.title: Cercospora Leaf Blight of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Light purple spots expand and deepen in color to reddish-purple or bronze on leaves. Infected leaves appear leathery and 'sunburned'. Under hot and humid conditions, foliar symptoms appear in upper canopy leaves and petioles. Reddish-purple lesions may occur on stems and pods. Infected seeds have pink to purple discoloration on seed coats.

candidate_sources.title: Cercospora leaf blight and purple seed stain on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Disease is characterized by small brown spots encircled with bronze-purple borders on leaf surface. As disease progresses, upper canopy develops bronze to purple coloration with leathery feel. Seeds on infected plants develop purple stain. Management includes resistant varieties, crop rotation, and integrated approaches combining cultural practices and fungicide applications.

candidate_sources.title: Cercospora kikuchii (purple seed stain) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Cercospora kikuchii is a fungal pathogen causing both leaf blight and purple seed stain in soybean, found almost worldwide. On leaves: purplish bronzing at seed set with necrotic lesions on upper foliage progressing downward. On seeds: irregular blotches from light to dark purple with wide cracks in seed coat. Management relies on fungicide applications; fungicide resistance is an emerging challenge.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Charcoal Rot | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Charcoal rot is caused by Macrophomina phaseolina. Symptoms include brown to dark spots on cotyledons at seedling stage, and light brown to grey superficial lesions on stems in mid to late season. Characteristic microsclerotia appear as tiny black specks in vascular tissue, resembling charcoal dust. Disease development is favored by hot, dry conditions and plant stress.

candidate_sources.title: Charcoal Rot in Soybean | Cooperative Extension | University of Delaware
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Delaware Cooperative Extension fact sheet on charcoal rot in soybean, providing detailed information on symptom identification, pathogen biology, and management strategies for this important soybean disease.

candidate_sources.title: Charcoal Rot on Soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Minnesota Extension guide on charcoal rot management in soybean, including identification of symptoms on roots and stems near the soil surface, pathogen characteristics, and integrated management approaches for soybean production.

candidate_sources.title: Phytophthora Damping-off and Root Rot of Soybean | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Phytophthora damping-off and root rot is caused by Phytophthora sojae. Seedlings affected by damping-off show soft, water-soaked rotting on the hypocotyl and roots, typically appearing brown or black. Disease is most common in cool, wet soil conditions. Management includes seed treatment with fungicides, use of resistant varieties, and improving soil drainage.

candidate_sources.title: Pythium Damping-off of Soybean | NDSU Agriculture
candidate_sources.snippet: Pythium damping-off of soybean is caused by Pythium species fungi. Symptoms include pre-emergent damping-off where seedlings rot before emergence, and post-emergent damping-off where seedlings collapse with soft, water-soaked lesions on the hypocotyl and roots. The characteristic symptom is soft, brownish-colored rotting tissue. Cool, wet soil conditions favor disease development.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Seed and Seedling Diseases | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Soybean seedling diseases (damping-off) are caused by a group of fungi including Rhizoctonia, Pythium, Phytophthora, and Fusarium acting independently or together. Symptoms include seed rot, hypocotyl cankers, root rot, and seedling collapse. Reddish-brown sunken lesions form on hypocotyls, with firm dry cankers that girdle seedlings. Disease is most common in cool, wet soils and poorly-drained fields.

candidate_sources.title: Downy mildew on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Small, light green spots on upper leaf surfaces that enlarge and turn pale to bright yellow. Tan to gray tufts of fungal growth develop on lower leaf surfaces under wet and humid conditions. Caused by Peronospora manshurica, a water mold pathogen requiring water or high humidity for infection.

candidate_sources.title: Downy Mildew - Soybean Disease - Soybean Research & Information Network - SRIN
candidate_sources.snippet: Downy mildew of soybean is caused by the fungal-like organism Peronospora manshurica. Symptoms include light green to yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces with tan to gray fungal growth on lower surfaces. Disease is most common after flowering begins and occurs during high humidity and moderate temperatures.

candidate_sources.title: Downy Mildew of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive encyclopedia entry dedicated to soybean downy mildew disease including symptom identification, pathogen biology, environmental conditions favoring disease development, and integrated management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Frogeye Leaf Spot of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Frogeye leaf spot is caused by the fungus Cercospora sojina. Early symptoms appear as small, dark, water-soaked, circular to angular lesions (1-5 mm diameter). Spots eventually enlarge to approximately ¼ inch with gray-brown centers and reddish-purple margins. Optimal conditions include temperatures of 77-86°F with high humidity (>90% RH). Management includes resistant variety selection, cultural practices, and fungicide applications.

candidate_sources.title: Frogeye leaf spot on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Frogeye leaf spot, caused by Cercospora sojina, presents as circular lesions with distinctive gray centers and reddish-brown margins. Symptoms are most visible in the upper canopy during reproductive growth stages. The fungus overwinters in crop residue and spreads via rain splash and air currents. Favorable conditions include high humidity and temperatures between 77-86°F (25-30°C).

candidate_sources.title: Frogeye Leaf Spot on Soybean | Cooperative Extension | University of Delaware
candidate_sources.snippet: Frogeye leaf spot is a fungal disease caused by Cercospora sojina affecting soybean crops. Disease symptoms develop as water-soaked lesions that enlarge and develop characteristic gray-brown centers with purple margins. Infection is favored by high humidity and moderate temperatures. Management strategies include crop rotation, residue removal, resistant varieties, and timely fungicide applications during reproductive stages.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Wilt of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium wilt is a disease complex caused by several soil-borne fungi, commonly Fusarium oxysporum. Symptoms include interveinal chlorosis, premature defoliation and wilting. Roots often decay with brown to black epidermal tissues and reddish to brown vascular discoloration extending into the stem.

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Root Rot and Wilt of Soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium root rot and wilt disease of soybean. Infection can occur at any growth stage, but more often at early vegetative and reproductive stages (V3 and R1). F. oxysporum produces different spore types (microconidia and macroconidia) and overwintering structures (chlamydospores).

candidate_sources.title: Fusarium Root Rot and Wilt of Soybean | Crop Protection Network
candidate_sources.snippet: Fusarium wilt often occurs in irregular patches in the field. Symptoms are often first observed in hot and dry conditions when plants struggle to take up water. Upper leaves may appear scorched while leaves in the middle and lower canopy turn chlorotic and wilt.

candidate_sources.title: Green stem syndrome on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Green stem syndrome refers to plants that maintain green stems and sometimes leaves well past the time when they are normally brown and mature, with plant stems remaining moist while the pods and seeds have ripened. The cause is unknown, and the incidence varies by location and cultivar. Management strategies include cultivar selection and stress management.

candidate_sources.title: Green Stem Syndrome in Soybean | Oklahoma State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Green stem syndrome in soybean is characterized by plants maintaining green stems and sometimes leaves well past maturity, with moist stems while pods and seeds are ripened. The cause is unknown but may result from viral infections, insect feeding, and environmental stresses. Management includes cultivar selection and stress management during pod fill.

candidate_sources.title: Green Stem Disorder of Soybean | Plant Disease - APS Journals
candidate_sources.snippet: Green Stem Disorder characterized by delayed senescence of stems with normal pod ripening. Research showed green stem disorder was independent of Bean pod mottle virus (BPMV) infection (P = 0.98). The cause of green stem disorder remains unknown, though multiple potential factors were investigated.

candidate_sources.title: Phymatotrichum Root Rot of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms are rapid wilting and death of plants, along with extensive root rot. A brown fungal growth may be seen on the surface of the roots. This disease usually occurs later in the soybean growing season, coinciding with high soil temperatures (90s°F) and is particularly severe following rain or irrigation.

candidate_sources.title: Phymatotrichum Root Rot | Oklahoma State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Phymatotrichum root rot is a soilborne disease caused by the fungus Phymatotrichopsis omnivora. The disease has been reported in Texas and some counties in Oklahoma and is associated with alkaline soils only. Management options for this disease are extremely limited with no fungicide labeled for control.

candidate_sources.title: Phymatotrichopsis omnivora (cotton root rot) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI datasheet covering the causal organism Phymatotrichopsis omnivora, including Identity, Overview, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts/Species Affected, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Impacts, and Prevention/Control measures for Phymatotrichum root rot across host crops.

candidate_sources.title: Pod and stem blight and phomopsis seed decay on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Pod and stem blight is caused by the fungus Diaporthe phaseolorum var. sojae. Symptoms include many small, black, raised dots (pycnidia) arranged in rows on infected stems, pods, and fallen petioles late in the season. Upper portions of infected plants may turn yellow and die. Infected seed are cracked, shriveled, dull, and may have a gray mold on them.

candidate_sources.title: Pod and Stem Blight | CropWatch | Nebraska
candidate_sources.snippet: Pod and stem blight is caused by the fungus Diaporthe phaseolorum var. sojae and Diaporthe longicolla. Management strategies include using high quality pathogen-free seed, rotating soybean with non-hosts such as wheat or corn, applying foliar or seed treatment fungicides, and harvesting seed quickly after maturity. Wet, warm conditions and continuous planting of soybeans favors the disease.

candidate_sources.title: Diaporthe phaseolorum var. sojae (pod blight: soyabean) | CABI
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet covering Identity, Overview, Associated Diseases, Distribution, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Seedborne Aspects, Impacts, and Prevention/Control measures for Diaporthe phaseolorum var. sojae, the causal agent of pod and stem blight of soybean.
diseases_mentioned: Pod and stem blight of soybean

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Powdery Mildew | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms include a white, powdery coating on infected leaves. White to gray powdery patches begin small but coalesce to cover the entire leaf as disease progresses. Infected leaves most common on lower and middle canopy. Caused by fungus Erysiphe diffusa (syn. Microsphaera diffusa). Management includes varietal resistance; chemical management not recommended as disease does not typically affect yields.

candidate_sources.title: Powdery mildew on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: White powdery patches of fungal mycelium and conidia form on upper leaf surfaces, stems and pods. Cooler temperatures of 65-77°F favor disease development. Yield losses measured up to 10 bushels per acre in Iowa and 5 bushels per acre in Wisconsin. Management includes resistant varieties and fungicide application (tebuconazole, carbendazim) at growth stage R4. Crop rotation not effective due to long-range wind-blown spore dispersal.

candidate_sources.title: Erysiphe diffusa (soybean powdery mildew) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive pathogen profile covering the fungus Erysiphe diffusa (formerly Microsphaera diffusa), an obligate biotrophic fungal pathogen causing powdery mildew of soybean and other legumes. Includes symptomatology, epidemiology, host range, environmental requirements, yield impact, and integrated management strategies with resistance breeding and chemical control options.

candidate_sources.title: Cercospora Leaf Blight and Purple Seed Stain of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Managing cercospora leaf blight requires an integrated approach combining cultural practices, resistant varieties and fungicide applications. Management includes: use pathogen-free seed and low-susceptibility varieties, crop rotation to corn or small grains for 1-2 years, incorporate residue to reduce inoculum, and apply seed treatment fungicides or foliar fungicides during R3-R5 growth stages to prevent pod infections.

candidate_sources.title: Screening a Diverse Soybean Germplasm Collection for Reaction to Purple Seed Stain Caused by Cercospora kikuchii
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed research on genetic screening for resistance to Purple Seed Stain caused by Cercospora kikuchii. Study evaluates diverse soybean germplasm collection for reactions to the disease, providing data on host resistance sources for breeding programs.

candidate_sources.title: Red Crown Rot of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Red crown rot, caused by the fungus Calonectria ilicicola, is a soilborne disease of soybean. The disease causes reddish discoloration of the crown and stem just above the soil line, interveinal chlorosis and necrosis of leaves, premature defoliation, and root rot. Perithecia (fruiting bodies) appear as bright, reddish-orange structures on the stem and crown. Management includes resistant varieties, crop rotation, and soil management practices.

candidate_sources.title: A Diagnostic Guide for Red Crown Rot of Soybean | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: This diagnostic guide provides comprehensive information on red crown rot of soybean caused by Calonectria ilicicola (anamorph: Cylindrocladium parasiticum). Symptoms include reddish-orange discoloration at the crown, gray-brown vascular discoloration when stems are split, severe root necrosis, and premature plant death. The pathogen produces microsclerotia that persist in soil for years.

candidate_sources.title: Red Crown Rot of Soybean: What To Do If You Suspect It Is In Your Field | Purdue University Pest&Crop newsletter
candidate_sources.snippet: Purdue Extension resources on red crown rot management in soybeans. The disease is identified by reddish-brown lesions at the crown and stem base, leaf chlorosis and necrosis, and wilting. Single plants or small patches appear randomly throughout fields, rarely exceeding 30% incidence. Early detection and field scouting are critical for managing this emerging disease.

candidate_sources.title: Rhizoctonia Damping-off and Root Rot of Soybeans
candidate_sources.snippet: Reddish-brown, sunken lesions form on hypocotyls of young seedlings. The resulting firm, dry canker can girdle the seedling and cause it to collapse. Rhizoctonia solani can infect soybeans across a wide temperature range (60-95°F) and wide range of soil moisture conditions. The pathogen can survive for years in the field as mycelium or sclerotia in soil.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Seedling Diseases
candidate_sources.snippet: NC State Extension comprehensive publication on soybean seedling diseases covering Rhizoctonia solani, Pythium species, and Fusarium species as causal agents. Details symptom descriptions, disease cycle, environmental conditions favoring disease development, and management recommendations including seed treatments and cultural practices.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean rust | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms begin on leaves in the lower plant canopy, with tan or reddish-brown lesions developing first on the underside of leaves. Small pustules develop in lesions, releasing masses of tan spores. Two species of rust fungi cause soybean rust: Phakopsora pachyrhizi (aggressive Asian pathogen) and P. meibomiae (mild pathogen). Extended periods of wet weather, moderate temperatures (59-85°F), and high humidity (>75%) favor disease development.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Rust | Ohioline - The Ohio State University
candidate_sources.snippet: Official Ohio State University factsheet on soybean rust identification and management. Covers symptom recognition on leaf undersides with tan/reddish-brown lesions, pathogen biology, disease conditions favoring spread, and management strategies including fungicide application timing and coverage requirements. Soybean rust can cause yield losses greater than 50% under favorable conditions.

candidate_sources.title: Asian Soybean Rust | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: North Carolina State University Extension publication dedicated to Asian Soybean Rust. Provides comprehensive diagnostic information for identifying Phakopsora pachyrhizi, describes optimal infection conditions, and discusses management recommendations. Includes integrated pest management strategies and monitoring protocols for early detection.

candidate_sources.title: Southern Blight of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Yellowing and wilting are usually the first symptoms observed. Light brown lesions develop on stems near soil surface that later darken. White, fan-like mat of hyphae develops on infected stems. Caused by Sclerotium rolfsii. Overwinters as sclerotia (3-4 years viable). Management: crop rotation to non-host crops like corn, grain sorghum, or wheat for 2+ years. Fungicides not recommended.

candidate_sources.title: Athelia rolfsii (sclerotium rot) - CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive datasheet covering Identity, Distribution, Hosts, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Environmental Requirements (hot 77-95°F and humid), Impacts, and Prevention/Control strategies. Host range of 200+ plant species. Sclerotia remain viable 3-4 years near soil surface. Provides detailed information on survival structures and disease management for affected crops including soybean.

candidate_sources.title: Southern Blight/Sclerotium Blight - UT Crops Pest Guides
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Tennessee pest guide for Southern Blight on soybean. White mat of fungal mycelium forms at stem base and on debris, with white, tan, or brown spherical sclerotia about bird seed size. Yellowing and wilting with light brown lesions on stems near soil surface. Disease favored by hot (77-95°F), humid weather. Sclerotia are overwintering structures. More susceptible in early growth stages.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean cyst nematode (SCN) | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Soybean cyst nematode is the most yield-limiting pathogen of soybean in the U.S. SCN is caused by the nematode Heterodera glycines. Symptoms include plant stunting, chlorosis (yellowing), and wilting. White or cream-colored lemon-shaped cysts may be visible on soybean roots. Often called a 'silent yield robber,' SCN can reduce yields without obvious aboveground symptoms.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Cyst Nematode - Extension Entomology
candidate_sources.snippet: Soybean Cyst Nematode (SCN), caused by Heterodera glycines, is a major pest of soybean. This Purdue Extension publication provides comprehensive management strategies including host resistance, crop rotation, and chemical treatments. Symptoms appear as patchy stunting and yellowing in fields.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Cyst Nematode | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: This comprehensive guide covers the biology, identification, and management of Soybean Cyst Nematode (Heterodera glycines). The pathogen causes yield losses through root damage. Management includes varietal resistance selection and crop rotation practices.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Cyst Nematode of Soybean: A Diagnostic Guide | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: Diagnostic guide for Soybean Cyst Nematode (Heterodera glycines) infection in soybean. This APS publication provides detailed identification methods, symptom descriptions, and laboratory diagnostic techniques for SCN detection and pathogen confirmation.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Dwarf Virus | Plant Health Cases
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Digital Library plant health case study on Soybean Dwarf Virus. Provides comprehensive information on symptoms, pathogen characteristics, and management strategies for this economically important soybean disease.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean dwarf virus
candidate_sources.snippet: PlantWise Plus Knowledge Bank species factsheet on Soybean dwarf virus. Documents symptoms including stunting, leaf rugosity, interveinal chlorosis, and transmission via aphids. First identified in northern Japan in 1969 with yield losses up to 80%.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Dwarf of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Crop Protection Network encyclopedia entry dedicated to Soybean Dwarf disease. Covers symptom manifestations including stunting, dark green brittle leaves, leaf curling, yellowing between veins, and management practices for affected soybean crops.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean mosaic virus | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Soybean mosaic is caused by the single-stranded positive-sense RNA soybean mosaic virus (SMV), a member of the genus Potyvirus. Symptoms range from no apparent symptoms to severely mottled and deformed leaves with light and dark green mottling. Trifoliate leaves develop a mosaic of light and dark green areas that may become blistered or raised, with leaves appearing distorted and margins curling downward. SMV is transmitted by aphids, sap, and infected seed, causing yield losses of 8-35%, with reports up to 94%.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Mosaic Virus | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: NC State Extension factsheet on Soybean Mosaic Virus (SMV) covering identification, symptoms, epidemiology, and management strategies for this important soybean pathogen affecting crop yield and plant health.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Vein Necrosis Virus | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Soybean vein necrosis virus (SVNV) is a Tospovirus that starts as randomly distributed, irregular yellow spots along major leaf veins that progress to red-brown, necrotic lesions. Symptoms range from thread-like vein clearing to necrosis covering most of a leaf. The virus is spread by immature soybean thrips and is more common during hot, dry summers when thrip activity is increased.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Vein Necrosis Virus
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Delaware Cooperative Extension factsheet providing comprehensive information on identification of soybean vein necrosis virus symptoms, disease cycle, host range, and current management strategies including thrips vector control and resistant variety selection.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean vein necrosis virus | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Compendium datasheet on soybean vein necrosis virus including comprehensive coverage of the pathogen (Orthotospovirus genus), geographic distribution, hosts, symptoms, transmission by thrips vectors, and integrated management recommendations for affected crops.

candidate_sources.title: Soybean Sudden Death Syndrome | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Sudden Death Syndrome (SDS) is a foliar disease that affects soybean. The causal agent is the soil-borne fungus Fusarium virguliforme. Symptoms include yellowing between leaf veins with necrotic lesions, and infected plants may show wilting and root rot.

candidate_sources.title: Sudden death syndrome on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: Sudden Death Syndrome of soybean is caused by Fusarium virguliforme (formerly F. solani f. sp. glycines). Root symptoms appear 2-3 weeks after germination but foliar symptoms appear later. A bluish mold on taproot is diagnostic. Foliar symptoms show interveinal chlorosis and necrotic lesions.

candidate_sources.title: Sudden Death Syndrome of Soybean | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Sudden Death Syndrome (SDS) is caused by the soil-borne fungus Fusarium virguliforme. The fungus infects roots early in the season but symptoms develop later as yellowing and necrosis between leaf veins. Management includes resistant varieties, crop rotation, and cultural practices.

candidate_sources.title: First Description of the Causal Agent of Taproot Decline of Soybean, an Emerging Disease in the Southern United States | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: First description of Xylaria necrophora as causal agent of taproot decline, an emerging disease in southern US. Describes symptoms including foliar interveinal chlorosis and necrosis, with darkened black stroma on taproots and lateral roots. Newly identified pathogen unique as only Xylaria species attacking annual crops.

candidate_sources.title: First Report of Taproot Decline Caused by Xylaria sp. on Soybean in Tennessee | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: First report of taproot decline caused by Xylaria sp. on soybean in Tennessee. Documents disease symptoms from V6 to R6 stages, pathogen identification, and geographic distribution extending from Mississippi River Valley to Alabama and southeastern Missouri.

candidate_sources.title: Unlocking the Mystery of Taproot Decline - Research Highlight - Soybean Research & Information Network - SRIN
candidate_sources.snippet: Research highlight on taproot decline pathology and management. Discusses symptom identification (yellowing leaves, dry brittle taproots), pathogen biology (Xylaria necrophora), and management strategies including effectiveness of tillage and crop rotation for reducing inoculum load.

candidate_sources.title: Target Spot of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Lesions are reddish-brown, round to irregularly shaped, often surrounded by yellow halos. Lesions vary in size, often ⅜ to ⅝ inch in diameter in the lower canopy. Concentric rings may form in developed lesions. Caused by Corynespora cassiicola. Requires wet conditions for infection. Management includes crop residue destruction and fungicide rotation due to QoI resistance.

candidate_sources.title: Target Spot of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Fungal disease caused by Corynespora cassiicola. Lesions are 10-15 mm in diameter with alternating concentric rings of light and dark brown bands, often surrounded by yellow halo. Overwinters in plant debris and soil. Disease resurgent in the Americas with yield losses between 10-42%. Management requires fungicides and cultural practices including crop residue destruction.

candidate_sources.title: Target Spot - UT Crops Pest Guides
candidate_sources.snippet: Foliar fungal disease of soybean caused by Corynespora cassiicola. Symptoms include circular lesions with concentric rings. Disease develops in warm (75-85°F), wet conditions with free leaf moisture. Most severe after canopy closure in mid to late season. Management through fungicide applications and crop rotation.

candidate_sources.title: Corynespora cassiicola (target leaf spot of tomato)
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI International Species Datasheet for Corynespora cassiicola, the fungal pathogen causing target spot. Host range includes over 500 plant species across 53 families. Conidia dispersed by water and air. Important host includes soybean with significant economic impact.

candidate_sources.title: Increased Occurrence of Target Spot of Soybean Caused by Corynespora cassiicola in the Southeastern United States | Plant Disease
candidate_sources.snippet: Peer-reviewed research documenting increased occurrence of target spot caused by Corynespora cassiicola in southeastern US soybean. Reports on disease resurgence and epidemiology. Published in Plant Disease journal by American Phytopathological Society.

candidate_sources.title: Tobacco Ringspot Virus of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Plants infected early may show signs of stunting, flower and bud proliferation, and shepherd's crooking of the terminal bud before other buds become necrotic and drop. Roots may be severely stunted with brown discoloration of stem pith, and some infected plants develop ringspots on their leaves. Pod development is poor in infected plants, with dark spots on the pods which may drop early or produce nonviable seeds. TRSV can be transmitted by some arthropods, such as thrips and grasshoppers, as well as the dagger nematode.

candidate_sources.title: Tobacco ringspot virus | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive datasheet covering Identity, Overview, Associated Diseases, Pests or Pathogens, Distribution, Dispersal, Hosts/Species Affected, Vectors & Intermediate Hosts, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Seedborne Aspects, and Impacts. Bud blight of soybean is the most severe disease caused by TRSV and causes the greatest losses, with yields potentially reduced by 25 to 100%. Management strategies include use of virus-free soybean seeds in commercial fields and avoidance of fields infested with dagger nematodes.

candidate_sources.title: Information on Tobacco Ringspot Virus, Laboratory for Soybean Disease Research, U of I
candidate_sources.snippet: University of Illinois Laboratory for Soybean Disease Research provides detailed information on Tobacco Ringspot Virus transmission, ecology, and disease management. TRSV is transmitted by dagger nematodes (Xiphinema americanum) and can be seed-borne, with virus remaining viable in seeds for years. Transmission from one season to the next can be caused by infected seed, and some soybean cultivars have shown resistance to certain strains of TRSV.

candidate_sources.title: Tobacco Streak of Soybean
candidate_sources.snippet: Tobacco Streak Virus (TSV) causes bud blight, stunting, necrotic spots on leaves and pods, delayed maturity, and reduced yields in soybean. TSV is transmitted by thrips and contaminated seed. Symptoms include shepherd's crook, wilting, and discolored streaks. The virus is seed transmitted and thrips are the primary vector. Management includes using certified seed, controlling thrips populations, and removing infected plants.

candidate_sources.title: Tobacco streak virus (tobacco streak) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Tobacco streak virus (TSV) is a plant pathogenic virus of the family Bromoviridae, in the genus Ilarvirus. It has a wide host range including soybean, peanuts, sunflower, cotton, and cranberry. Economically important symptoms include bud blight, stunting, reduced plant height and density, and delayed seed development. Transmission occurs through infected seed and by thrips vectors. The virus causes significant yield losses in soybean and other legume crops.

candidate_sources.title: Re-emergence of Tobacco streak virus Infecting Soybean in the United States and Canada | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: Tobacco streak virus has re-emerged as an important pathogen of soybean in the United States and Canada. The virus causes bud blight, necrotic spots on pods and leaves, stem discoloration, reduced pod number per plant, and delayed seed maturation. TSV is transmitted by thrips and through infected soybean seed. Recent outbreaks have been reported in Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Wisconsin, and Ontario, Canada. Management strategies include seed treatment and thrips control.

candidate_sources.title: Sclerotinia stem rot (white mold) on soybean | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: White mold is caused by the soilborne fungus Sclerotinia sclerotiorum. Symptoms include water-soaked lesions on the main stem that expand and become bleached, with fluffy white mycelium and black sclerotia visible in moist conditions. Disease development is favored by wet conditions and cool temperatures during flowering.

candidate_sources.title: White Mold of Soybean | NC State Extension Publications
candidate_sources.snippet: Detailed factsheet on White Mold of Soybean covering symptom identification on stems, petioles and pods, the soilborne pathogen Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, disease cycle and epidemiology, and management strategies including fungicide application and varietal resistance.

candidate_sources.title: Sclerotinia Stem Rot (White Mold) of Soybean | Ohioline
candidate_sources.snippet: Ohio State's factsheet on Sclerotinia stem rot (white mold) describing characteristic bleached lesions with white fungal growth, disease development during flowering, conditions favoring infection (wet and cool), and integrated management approaches including cultural practices and fungicide recommendations.
